title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?

paper.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?
paper.abstract: Abstract Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model’s own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Video world models are expected to capture regularities that make visual futures predictable. Prediction errors and related scores are consequently used to assess physical plausibility and identify unexpected events ( Smith et al., 2019 ; Piloto et al., 2022 ; Riochet et al., 2018 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Garrido et al., 2025 ; Bordes et al., 2025 ; Maes et al., 2026 ) . Such scores also guide the selection of physically plausible generated videos ( Baldassarre et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Understanding what they measure matters when errors are used to locate events, compare videos, or reward trajectories. Let f C f_{C} and f T f_{T} construct context and target latent representations, also called features, from observations x x . Both functions include the model’s encoding and token-selection steps. For a predictor p p , optional actions a a , and a scoring distance d d , the prediction-error score is S ⁡ ( x , a ) = d ⁡ ( p ⁡ ( f C ​ ( x ) , a ) , f T ​ ( x ) ) . S(x,a)=d\!\left(p(f_{C}(x),a),\,f_{T}(x)\right). This score measures prediction difficulty in the chosen representation. A large value may reflect physical inconsistency, appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary model error. Physical information may also be accessible to a classifier even when the predictor’s error responds primarily to other properties of the video. We first test whether linear classifiers can distinguish physically possible from impossible events using frozen representations. We also test how well appearance information can be recovered from the same representations. IntPhys2 is a synthetic video benchmark pairing physically possible events with violations such as an object passing through a solid obstacle ( Bordes et al., 2025 ) . We compare V-JEPA2-G, trained to predict latent representations, with VideoMAE2-G, trained to reconstruct masked pixels, and simple visual statistics. Linear classifiers readily recover appearance labels from all three. V-JEPA2-G provides a modest advantage when classifying events as possible or impossible. We then examine how appearance and physical differences are organized across network depth. Changes in hue, brightness, and object color let us measure how far representations move, how consistently they move in the same direction across scenes, and how much those directions overlap with differences between possible and impossible events. In both V-JEPA2-G and VideoMAE2-G, appearance shifts become smaller relative to distances between unrelated videos. At deeper layers, the shifts line up more than those from randomly paired videos and overlap less with physical changes, though these trends sometimes reverse between layers. Appearance labels nevertheless remain easy to recover at the evaluated probe layers. We also test whether representation distances help predict changes in V-JEPA2-G’s prediction error. In a regression analysis, they add little beyond scene conditions and simple visual statistics. Finally, we test prediction error under controlled changes to actions, appearance, motion, and physical validity. Across three action-conditioned world models, incorrect actions raise error while the observed frames are held fixed. Color changes also alter error without changing the simulated physical state. In Physion++ videos of physical interactions, repeating a single frame can increase error, whereas changing color throughout a clip can lower it ( Tung et al., 2023 ) . Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we test stopping and falling with and without support beneath an object ( Greff et al., 2022 ) . Mean error is higher for stopping in both settings, even though stopping is lawful only when support is present. A fixed error threshold also flags many lawful events as impossible. These results show why recoverable physical information and action sensitivity alone are insufficient to interpret prediction error as physical surprise.

sections.heading: Predictive video representations.
sections.text: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting latent representations rather than pixels ( LeCun, 2022 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) . V-JEPA2 extends this approach to video understanding, prediction, and planning ( Assran et al., 2025 ) , while VideoMAE and VideoMAE2 learn representations through masked pixel reconstruction ( Tong et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . Action-conditioned models such as LeWorldModel, DINO-WM, and JEPA-WM predict visual representations from observations and actions ( Maes et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Terver et al., 2026 ) . These objectives provide different representations and native error scales. Our comparisons retain each released pipeline and test the meaning of its error through controlled interventions.

sections.heading: Physical information and latent geometry.
sections.text: Inverse-dynamics probes recover actions from video representations ( Yeom et al., 2026 ) ; robotic evaluations distinguish representations useful for reconstruction from those useful for planning ( Nilaksh et al., 2026 ) . Layerwise probes and subspace analyses reveal physics-related structure in V-JEPA2 and VideoMAE2 ( Joseph et al., 2026 ; Punzo et al., 2026 ) . Geometry regularization can improve multistep prediction ( Xia et al., 2026 ) , and PhyLatent studies physical invariance and identifiability under appearance and dynamics changes ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) . We connect this representation-level evidence to a separate question: whether measured geometry predicts native-error differences in the same model and setting.

sections.heading: Physical prediction and violation of expectation.
sections.text: IntPhys and IntPhys2 evaluate possible versus impossible events ( Riochet et al., 2018 ; Bordes et al., 2025 ) ; Physion and Physion++ evaluate physical-outcome prediction and inference of latent physical properties ( Bear et al., 2021 ; Tung et al., 2023 ) . Violation-of-expectation models use predicted-versus-observed discrepancies to identify unexpected physical events ( Smith et al., 2019 ; Piloto et al., 2022 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Garrido et al., 2025 ) . Related evaluations address counterfactual consistency and physical plausibility in generated videos ( Begiristain et al., 2026 ; Baldassarre et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . We focus on the specificity and transfer of a fixed native score: whether physical violations increase error across controlled changes in motion, appearance, and context.

sections.heading: 3 Evaluation framework
sections.text: We retain each evaluated pipeline’s encoders, token selection, normalization, and native distance. Context-only prediction and encoding a full clip before selecting context tokens are distinct computations (Section 4.2 ). Native score magnitudes are compared only within a model. Table 1 separates evidence about representations from evidence about the score. Readout and geometry characterize encoded information; the remaining checks test predictive sensitivity and physical decisions. For threshold-based detection, a lawful clip above the threshold is a false alarm, and an impossible clip below it is a missed violation. Table 1: Six complementary checks for interpreting prediction error as physical surprise. Calibration here means transfer of a fixed decision threshold, rather than calibration of predicted probabilities. Check Controlled comparison and measured property Readout Train a linear classifier on frozen representations and test it on scenes excluded from training. Measure how accurately it distinguishes physically possible from impossible events. Geometry Measure appearance and physical shifts across layers. Relative size shows how strongly appearance changes affect representations compared with differences between unrelated videos. Stronger alignment than in shuffled pairs indicates a consistent response across scenes. Greater overlap than with random subspaces of the same dimension indicates shared directions between appearance and physical changes. Action Keep the observed outcome fixed and compare predictions made with correct and mismatched actions. Check whether incorrect actions increase prediction error. Appearance/static Change appearance without changing the simulated physical state, or repeat a single frame throughout a clip. Compare prediction error with the original clip. Physical validity Compare possible and impossible events while varying motion or appearance. Check whether impossible events consistently receive higher error within each condition. Calibration Choose an error threshold on separate calibration data and apply it unchanged to new scenes and appearances. Measure the rates of false alarms and missed violations. We evaluate V-JEPA2-G on controlled Kubric videos and IntPhys2, V-JEPA2-L on Physion++ Mass, and released action-conditioned models on TwoRoom and PushT. The IntPhys2 comparison includes VideoMAE2-G and low-level visual statistics. DINO-WM and JEPA-WM share a frozen DINOv2 encoder ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , so their comparison varies only the predictor. Uncertainty is estimated by bootstrap over independent configurations, Physion++ matched pairs within scenarios, IntPhys2 scenes, or action-test episodes. All conditions belonging to one unit remain together. Bonferroni-adjusted intervals are used for the specified families of contrasts. Thresholds and regression coefficients are fitted on data separate from evaluation. Full protocols, fitting and split histories, and reproducibility records are in the appendices. Code and numeric experiment records are available at https://github.com/3-ml/jepa-surprise (Appendix G ).

sections.heading: 4.1 Physical-violation ordering and threshold transfer
sections.text: To separate physical validity from trajectory identity, we render a falling sphere above either a solid platform or an opening. Each setting has two continuations: the sphere stops at platform height or falls below it. Stopping is lawful on the solid platform and unsupported over the opening; falling is lawful through the opening and violates solidity when it passes through the platform. Figure 8 in the appendix shows the rendered construction. The 256 configurations cross these four cases with the original appearance, a 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} hue shift throughout the clip (persistent), or the same shift starting at the target interval (abrupt), giving 3,072 clips. Stopping trajectories match across settings, as do falling trajectories. Within each setting and appearance, the two continuations share context frames and predictor outputs. Support appearance, shadows, and occlusion differ across settings. The predictor observes the first 12 of 48 frames; native error is mean absolute difference from normalized EMA-target tokens for the remaining 36 frames. V-JEPA2-G gives stopping higher mean error in both settings. Consequently, impossible-minus-possible error is negative on solid support and positive over the gap (Figure 1 ). The native score’s ordering follows the trajectory across this reversal of physical validity (Appendix Figure 9 ). Figure 1: V-JEPA2-G on 256 configurations. Left: impossible minus possible native error, with 98.75% configuration-bootstrap intervals adjusted for four means. The sign reverses between solid support and a gap. Right: balanced accuracy under a single threshold fitted on separate calibration scenes, with descriptive 95% configuration-bootstrap intervals. The dashed line marks 50%. The reversal holds under both clean and persistent-hue appearance; all four adjusted intervals exclude zero in their respective directions. Averaging the two settings would conceal the opposite orderings. Appendix E.2 reports the complete margins and intervals. A single threshold fitted on 24 separate clean calibration configurations yields 53.9% balanced accuracy [52.1, 55.8] on clean evaluation clips, with equal weight to both support settings. Performance differs sharply by setting: 80.7% over gaps versus 27.1% on solid support. The threshold falsely flags about 69% of lawful clips, including every lawful solid-support continuation (Appendix Figure 10 ). Thus the above-chance average coexists with a large false-alarm rate. Figure 1 also shows transfer under persistent and abrupt hue; Appendix E.2 gives all per-setting rates and the threshold definition.

sections.heading: 4.2 Static-content and persistent-appearance controls
sections.text: We evaluate V-JEPA2-L’s full-clip masked-prediction score on the 192 official Physion++ Mass videos. The encoder processes each 16-frame window before context tokens are selected, so target frames can influence the predictor. The static diagnostic compares every complete, nonoverlapping window with versions repeating its first, middle, or last frame. These still-frame controls have higher mean error than the original videos. Across videos, the mean share of windows scoring no higher than their average static baseline is approximately 84%. The mean original-minus-static difference is negative in every scenario, and the layout-cluster sensitivity check agrees. Uncertainty is based on scenario-stratified matched pairs, with windows averaged within videos, not treated as independent observations. Repeating frames changes both content and history, so this comparison neither isolates motion’s causal effect nor supplies a universal score correction. Persistent appearance changes can also lower error. This separate experiment uses one fixed middle 16-frame window per video. Hue shifts and pixel darkening applied throughout the window both lower mean error relative to the original and to their target-only counterparts (Table 2 ). Changes restricted to the final four frames have uncertain original-relative effects: their adjusted intervals include zero. The persistent-versus-target-only hue ordering reverses in Collision, so the overall mean does not describe every scenario. The normalized L1 score averages spatial-token errors over the two target frame-pairs (temporal tubelets). Because the encoder sees the full window, target-only edits can affect the predictor despite unchanged context pixels. These are diagnostics of the evaluated masked-prediction implementation. sections.heading: 4.3 Physical-label and appearance readouts
sections.text: Linear probes readily recover appearance labels. For V-JEPA2-G, physical-label accuracy under these probes is only modestly above chance: approximately 58% for possible versus impossible events, against 50% chance (Table 3 ). Its four-class appearance accuracy is approximately 98%, but the two tasks do not provide a common scale for the amount of information encoded. The physics result shows that label information is accessible. Whether native prediction error detects violations is a separate question, which the later experiments test. IntPhys2 tests object permanence, continuous motion, solidity, and constant object properties ( Bordes et al., 2025 ) . For example, a solidity pair contrasts a solid object stopping at an obstacle with one passing through it. We compare V-JEPA2-G and VideoMAE2-G with PixelSummary (RGB statistics, color histograms, and frame differences). Five-fold scene cross-fitting keeps each scene’s pairs and appearances together, with class-balanced linear probes and training-only feature scaling. sections.heading: 4.4 Layerwise representation geometry
sections.text: Both models show smaller final-layer appearance shifts relative to between-video differences than at the first layer (Figure 2 A). Relative magnitude divides each shift by the median unrelated-video distance at that layer. V-JEPA2-G’s hue ratio falls from approximately 57% to 8%. The measures compare V-JEPA2-G and VideoMAE2-G on the same 57 IntPhys2 scenes. Figure 2: Representation geometry on 57 IntPhys2 scenes. A: displacement relative to the median unrelated-video distance (log axis). B: directional coherence (mean resultant length, MRL) above shuffled correspondences. C: fraction of squared physical-pair displacement captured by a four-dimensional appearance subspace fitted on other scenes, with scene-bootstrap intervals and an equal-rank random reference. Directional coherence measures alignment across videos. At later depths, appearance shifts are more aligned relative to shuffled source-transform pairings, whereas physical-change directions remain closer to that reference (Figure 2 B). Subspace overlap measures the fraction of squared physical-feature change projected into an appearance subspace fitted on other scenes. Final overlap is lower than initial overlap, but the trajectory is not monotonic. V-JEPA2-G’s final overlap is approximately 6%, above the roughly 0.28% dimension-matched random reference (Figure 2 C). Appendix B.3 gives the complete geometry and source-video retrieval results.

sections.heading: 4.5 Predicting native-error differences from geometry
sections.text: We next test whether geometric measurements predict native-error differences in the crossed-support setting. Ordinary least squares (OLS) models fitted on 24 separate configurations predict physical margins (impossible minus lawful error) and appearance-induced score changes on the 256-configuration evaluation population. The baseline uses condition labels and static, motion, and shuffled-frame statistics; the expanded model adds relative representation distances and interactions with support or appearance timing. This compares geometry with information already available from the experimental conditions and visible changes. Adding final-encoder geometry changes physical-margin R 2 R^{2} from approximately 0.771 to 0.774, but the adjusted improvement interval includes both gains and losses. Some earlier locations worsen prediction. Here R 2 R^{2} uses the error of predicting the fitting-set mean as its denominator, rather than the evaluation-set mean. For appearance-score differences, both models perform worse than that reference. Across all five locations and both tasks, no improvement interval lies entirely above zero (Appendix Tables 23 – 24 ). This post-hoc analysis gives limited evidence of added predictive value from the tested geometry features and linear models. Native prediction error is the world model’s discrepancy between predicted and observed representations; the regression error here measures how well a separate model predicts differences in that discrepancy. Configuration-bootstrap intervals condition on the fitted regressions. Appendix F.1 (Figure 12 ) gives the full protocol and analysis history.

sections.heading: 4.6 Action and appearance sensitivity
sections.text: All three action-conditioned models use the supplied action: incorrect actions increase prediction error when the observed outcome is held fixed. We test 256 episodes per task or scorer under correct, zero, and reversed actions. LeWorldModel (LeWM) uses task-specific released checkpoints; DINO-WM and JEPA-WM reuse the PushT target frames and action interventions with their own preprocessing and predictors. Table 4 reports positive reversed-minus-correct contrasts for every model. Color changes also raise error while simulator state is held fixed. Figure 3 measures each hue change relative to the unchanged static target, and each action mismatch relative to the lawful prediction of the same moving target. sections.heading: 4.7 Task-associated color controls
sections.text: In a separate PushT study with simulator state fixed and RGB change matched, LeWM’s error still depends on color choice. Agent-blue blocks score higher than novel-orange blocks; block-gray agents likewise exceed matched purple. The target-only blue/orange gap is positive in 233 of 256 episodes. Persistent changes reduce the mean gaps but retain both orderings (Appendix C.2 ). For target-only edits, the prediction is unchanged and differences in target-encoder shifts account for almost all of the score gaps algebraically. Role colors can carry task information. These controls therefore show that the score depends on color. They leave open whether that color information helps predict physical outcomes and whether LeWorldModel encodes task roles.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: Physical labels can be read out of V-JEPA2-G representations (about 58% accuracy against 50% chance), yet its native prediction error does not consistently track physical validity in the crossed-support test. Appearance remains decodable even as its relative displacement decreases across depth, while physical labels are modestly accessible under the evaluated probes. These findings describe the representation, but do not determine which video changes produce large native errors. The same-model regression makes that connection explicit: the selected geometry features add little predictive value beyond visual statistics and experimental conditions. The native-error controls identify several sources of discrepancy. A score can remain high when motion is removed, or decrease after a persistent color change. In the crossed-support test, a stable trajectory ordering produces opposite physical-violation orderings and poor shared-threshold performance. Abrupt recoloring asks a different question: an unexpected color transition may itself violate object-property constancy. Persistent transformations remove that transition, allowing sensitivity to a stable appearance change to be examined separately. In PushT, the moving lawful targets already have higher error than the static ones. Comparing absolute scores can therefore rank the action change above the hue change, even though the hue increase over its own baseline is larger. Table 5 summarizes what each setting establishes. The evaluation framework turns the broad question of physical understanding into testable claims about a particular score. For a physical-surprise application, the decisive checks are violation ordering within relevant conditions and false-alarm and miss rates when a fixed decision rule transfers across them. sections.heading: 6 Limitations
sections.text: The controlled support experiment samples one procedural family with restricted cameras, colors, and lighting. It tests transfer across those conditions only; real-world and material generalization are untested. Material appearance can convey mass or friction cues, and greater training diversity may change appearance sensitivity. Those questions require additional data and controlled model comparisons. The IntPhys2 readout and geometry-to-error transfer are post-hoc analyses. Their intervals condition on fitted models and omit refitting uncertainty; the readout also conditions on fold assignments. The tested linear geometry models do not establish a mechanism or the effect of removing appearance directions. Physion++ provides contact labels and no physical-violation labels, and its full-clip scoring implementation permits target information to affect context tokens. These distinctions constrain the interpretation of each result. Model comparisons also vary architecture, pretraining, capacity, and native score. We do not estimate a general limit on planning or anomaly-detection performance. Application-specific acceptable error rates were not specified. Detailed split histories, failed compatibility checks, and excluded follow-ups are retained in the appendix.

sections.heading: Broader impact.
sections.text: Prediction errors can serve as measures of physical surprise when controlled tests establish what they respond to. Their use as rewards or safety signals requires validation in the intended task and environment.

sections.heading: Criteria for the main-text evidence table.
sections.text: In Table 5 , support refers to the inference named in Table 1 . IntPhys2 readout support is post-hoc, and geometry support concerns measured representation structure. The separate crossed-support geometry-to-error regression is not a second test of that structural criterion. Its result is discussed in Section 4.5 . The physical-validity check fails in the crossed-support experiment because violation margins have opposite signs across support conditions. Calibration remains insufficient: the fixed threshold makes frequent errors and no application-specific acceptable-error margin was specified. The Physion++ entry concerns the full-clip score; the action-model entries use the historical controls and the baseline decomposition in Appendix C.1.2 . sections.heading: B.1 IntPhys2 readout protocol and uncertainty
sections.text: The corrected IntPhys2 sealed test contains 114 matched possible/impossible pairs from 57 held-out scenes, 228 source videos, and 912 appearance-conditioned samples. Each sample uses exactly 64 decoded source frames sampled by rounded linear spacing. The four appearance conditions are clean, 90-degree hue rotation, brightness multiplier 0.45, and 180-degree selective recoloring. V-JEPA2-G and VideoMAE2-G are extracted at five frozen depths ( block_00 , block_10 , block_20 , block_30 , final ); PixelSummary is a 100-dimensional low-level baseline of RGB summary, color-histogram, and frame-difference statistics. The probe is StandardScaler plus balanced logistic regression with C = 1.0 C=1.0 and at most 2000 iterations. The post-hoc correction reported here sorts scenes by hash (seed 0) and splits them into five folds. The fold index (0 to 4) is also the classifier’s random state. Fold k k is test, fold ( k + 1 ) mod 5 (k+1)\bmod 5 is validation, and the remaining folds are training. Sealed test folds contain 12, 12, 11, 11, and 11 scenes; development test folds contain 8, 8, 8, 7, and 7, with all pair IDs and appearance variants from one scene held together. Primary layers preserve the original development choices: V-JEPA2-G block_20 for appearance and block_30 for physics, VideoMAE2-G block_30 for appearance, block_00 for all-appearance physics, and block_30 for clean-only physics, with PixelSummary using its only layer. The cross-fit development check retains V-JEPA2-G block_20 for appearance and block_30 for physics_all ; its all-appearance comparator deltas include zero. Brightness strength is 1 − b 1-b . Scene is the independent unit and intervals use 10,000 bootstrap draws. We use these trajectories to probe transformation geometry and local equivariance descriptively [ Lenc and Vedaldi, 2015 ] . Displacement dimensionality uses entropy effective rank, exp [ − ∑ j p j log p j ] \exp[-\sum_{j}p_{j}\log p_{j}] , where p j p_{j} is normalized squared singular-value energy. sections.heading: C.1.2 Separating target difficulty from intervention effects
sections.text: Let S 0 S_{0} denote the static lawful score, S h S_{h} the hue-modified static score, S l S_{l} the moving lawful score, and S o S_{o} the score for that same moving target under the opposite action. The reported cross-target contrast decomposes as S h − S o = ( S h − S 0 ) − ( S o − S l ) − ( S l − S 0 ) . S_{h}-S_{o}=(S_{h}-S_{0})-(S_{o}-S_{l})-(S_{l}-S_{0}). sections.heading: D.2 Historical static-audit selection and scoring
sections.text: The checkpoint identity is recorded in the online checkpoint table . Ten additional Physion++ Mass test videos were selected deterministically as evenly spaced files after excluding the earlier single-video debug example. Every complete 16-frame segment was scored, yielding 273 segments. For each segment we record the native latent residual, mean consecutive absolute RGB difference on the 0-255 scale, and the fraction of pixels whose consecutive-frame change exceeds 5. For static calibration, the first, middle, or last decoded frame is repeated across all 16 input positions and rescored. The first-frame event residual is the original score minus the corresponding frozen-frame score. This control does not estimate a universal corrected surprise score; it asks only whether a local raw peak requires temporal change.

Affiliation: Technology School Electronic Systems (TUES) Aleksandar Slavov 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Baba Tonka High School of Mathematics Vasil Vasilev 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Technology School Electronic Systems (TUES) Abstract Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model’s own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise. 1 Introduction Video world models are expected to capture regularities that make visual futures predictable. Prediction errors and related scores are consequently used to assess physical plausibility and identify unexpected events ( Smith et al., 2019 ; Piloto et al., 2022 ; Riochet et al., 2018 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Garrido et al., 2025 ; Bordes et al., 2025 ; Maes et al., 2026 ) . Such scores also guide the selection of physically plausible generated videos ( Baldassarre et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Understanding what they measure matters when errors are used to locate events, compare videos, or reward trajectories. Let f C f_{C} and f T f_{T} construct context and target latent representations, also called features, from observations x x . Both functions include the model’s encoding and token-selection steps. For a predictor p p , optional actions a a , and a scoring distance d d , the prediction-error score is S ⁡ ( x , a ) = d ⁡ ( p ⁡ ( f C ​ ( x ) , a ) , f T ​ ( x ) ) . S(x,a)=d\!\left(p(f_{C}(x),a),\,f_{T}(x)\right). This score measures prediction difficulty in the chosen representation. A large value may reflect physical inconsistency, appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary model error. Physical information may also be accessible to a classifier even when the predictor’s error responds primarily to other properties of the video. We first test whether linear classifiers can distinguish physically possible from impossible events using frozen representations. We also test how well appearance information can be recovered from the same representations. IntPhys2 is a synthetic video benchmark pairing physically possible events with violations such as an object passing through a solid obstacle ( Bordes et al., 2025 ) . We compare V-JEPA2-G, trained to predict latent representations, with VideoMAE2-G, trained to reconstruct masked pixels, and simple visual statistics. Linear classifiers readily recover appearance labels from all three. V-JEPA2-G provides a modest advantage when classifying events as possible or impossible. We then examine how appearance and physical differences are organized across network depth. Changes in hue, brightness, and object color let us measure how far representations move, how consistently they move in the same direction across scenes, and how much those directions overlap with differences between possible and impossible events. In both V-JEPA2-G and VideoMAE2-G, appearance shifts become smaller relative to distances between unrelated videos. At deeper layers, the shifts line up more than those from randomly paired videos and overlap less with physical changes, though these trends sometimes reverse between layers. Appearance labels nevertheless remain easy to recover at the evaluated probe layers. We also test whether representation distances help predict changes in V-JEPA2-G’s prediction error. In a regression analysis, they add little beyond scene conditions and simple visual statistics. Finally, we test prediction error under controlled changes to actions, appearance, motion, and physical validity. Across three action-conditioned world models, incorrect actions raise error while the observed frames are held fixed. Color changes also alter error without changing the simulated physical state. In Physion++ videos of physical interactions, repeating a single frame can increase error, whereas changing color throughout a clip can lower it ( Tung et al., 2023 ) . Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we test stopping and falling with and without support beneath an object ( Greff et al., 2022 ) . Mean error is higher for stopping in both settings, even though stopping is lawful only when support is present. A fixed error threshold also flags many lawful events as impossible. These results show why recoverable physical information and action sensitivity alone are insufficient to interpret prediction error as physical surprise. 2 Related work Predictive video representations. Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting latent representations rather than pixels ( LeCun, 2022 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) . V-JEPA2 extends this approach to video understanding, prediction, and planning ( Assran et al., 2025 ) , while VideoMAE and VideoMAE2 learn representations through masked pixel reconstruction ( Tong et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . Action-conditioned models such as LeWorldModel, DINO-WM, and JEPA-WM predict visual representations from observations and actions ( Maes et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Terver et al., 2026 ) . These objectives provide different representations and native error scales. Our comparisons retain each released pipeline and test the meaning of its error through controlled interventions. Physical information and latent geometry. Inverse-dynamics probes recover actions from video representations ( Yeom et al., 2026 ) ; robotic evaluations distinguish representations useful for reconstruction from those useful for planning ( Nilaksh et al., 2026 ) . Layerwise probes and subspace analyses reveal physics-related structure in V-JEPA2 and VideoMAE2 ( Joseph et al., 2026 ; Punzo et al., 2026 ) . Geometry regularization can improve multistep prediction ( Xia et al., 2026 ) , and PhyLatent studies physical invariance and identifiability under appearance and dynamics changes ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) . We connect this representation-level evidence to a separate question: whether measured geometry predicts native-error differences in the same model and setting. Physical prediction and violation of expectation. IntPhys and IntPhys2 evaluate possible versus impossible events ( Riochet et al., 2018 ; Bordes et al., 2025 ) ; Physion and Physion++ evaluate physical-outcome prediction and inference of latent physical properties ( Bear et al., 2021 ; Tung et al., 2023 ) . Violation-of-expectation models use predicted-versus-observed discrepancies to identify unexpected physical events ( Smith et al., 2019 ; Piloto et al., 2022 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Garrido et al., 2025 ) . Related evaluations address counterfactual consistency and physical plausibility in generated videos ( Begiristain et al., 2026 ; Baldassarre et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . We focus on the specificity and transfer of a fixed native score: whether physical violations increase error across controlled changes in motion, appearance, and context. 3 Evaluation framework We retain each evaluated pipeline’s encoders, token selection, normalization, and native distance. Context-only prediction and encoding a full clip before selecting context tokens are distinct computations (Section 4.2 ). Native score magnitudes are compared only within a model. Table 1 separates evidence about representations from evidence about the score. Readout and geometry characterize encoded information; the remaining checks test predictive sensitivity and physical decisions. Appearance remains decodable even as its relative displacement decreases across depth, while physical labels are modestly accessible under the evaluated probes. These findings describe the representation, but do not determine which video changes produce large native errors. The same-model regression makes that connection explicit: the selected geometry features add little predictive value beyond visual statistics and experimental conditions. The native-error controls identify several sources of discrepancy. A score can remain high when motion is removed, or decrease after a persistent color change. In the crossed-support test, a stable trajectory ordering produces opposite physical-violation orderings and poor shared-threshold performance. Abrupt recoloring asks a different question: an unexpected color transition may itself violate object-property constancy. Persistent transformations remove that transition, allowing sensitivity to a stable appearance change to be examined separately. In PushT, the moving lawful targets already have higher error than the static ones. Comparing absolute scores can therefore rank the action change above the hue change, even though the hue increase over its own baseline is larger. Table 5 summarizes what each setting establishes. The evaluation framework turns the broad question of physical understanding into testable claims about a particular score. For a physical-surprise application, the decisive checks are violation ordering within relevant conditions and false-alarm and miss rates when a fixed decision rule transfers across them. It tests transfer across those conditions only; real-world and material generalization are untested. Material appearance can convey mass or friction cues, and greater training diversity may change appearance sensitivity. Those questions require additional data and controlled model comparisons.
